newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil may become largest cotton importer in '97.
newsitem.headline: Brazil may become largest cotton importer in '97.

text.p: Brazil could become the world's largest importer of cotton in 1997 with domestic production set to drop to a 17-year low as farmers ditch cotton in favor of more profitable crops like soybeans, industry sources said.
Total Brazilian cotton production will be just 343,900 tonnes in 1996/97 with a planted area of 742,600 hectares, according to the Ministry of Agriculture's National Supply Company (Conab).

This means that Brazil would have to import around 500,000 tonnes in order to satisfy internal demand, outpacing China and Indonesia to become the world's biggest buyer of the commodity, traders said.
"We are already the second largest importer and we are on the way to becoming the first," said Hugo Sergio Nieri of brokerage Nieri Corretora.
Various factors are being blamed for the steady decline in planted area which turned Brazil from a net exporter of cotton into an importer in the early 90s.
These include a lack of financing for small producers who cannot compete with the payment conditions offered by foreign firms.

"Brazil used to be self-sufficient in cotton," said Renato Teixeira da Costa of Brazil's commodities and futures exchange BM&F. "Because of financing, cultivation has been splintered and there has been an enormous drop in planted area."

With international firms offering a payment period of 360 days at eight percent interest per year, small producers cannot compete. They need to charge a minimum of five percent interest a month in order to break even, said Nieri.
Even though Brazil had the conditions to produce a decent-sized cotton harvest, it was more profitable for farmers to plant other crops.

In addition, the cotton import market is practically deregulated although analysts think the introduction on Januaryu 1 of a new electronic import registration system, Siscomex, could change that situation.

Glitches with the new system have blocked cargoes of cotton and other goods at ports and borders. Traders' main complaint was that poor communications were preventing them from entering their import requests into a central computer.
"Everything is blocked," said a trader at an international firm. "You have trucks stuck at the border with Uruguay and cargoes blocked in ports and there is a very serious lack of organisation."
"If this goes on for another 15 days we will have real problems," he warned.

Although some traders believe the government is using the system to restore Brazil's ailing trade balance, most expect the start-up problems to be resolved soon, leaving traders to import as much cotton as they like.
"The government needs to introduce more drastic measures in future to slow the flow of imports," said Jose Sidnei Goncalves at the Sao Paulo agricultural secretariat.
In the meantime, traders are betting on a combination of the supply bottleneck and low industry stocks to aggressively bid for government stocks of cotton.
Last year's 415,000 tonne crop is sold out and traders are waiting for the first of the new harvest to hit the market in March.
"Depending on who you are talking about, some have four months' supply in stock and others have just 10 to 15 days," said one trader.

Traders bought nearly 50 percent of the 3,436 tonnes of cotton offered in an auction of government stocks on Wednesday, with prices rising to nearly 87 cents a lb excluding the cost of freight and of removing the stock from warehouses.
Internal prices are currently oscillating between 85 and 90 cents a lb, compared to 75 cents for the March contract in New York.
